lesson.title: An Infinite Tail: Building the Geometric Distribution
lesson.summary: The geometric distribution assigns a probability to every possible waiting time for a first success, an unbounded list of outcomes that still sums to exactly 1.
lesson.body:
In a geometric setting, let X denote the trial number on which the first success occurs. If the first success happens on the very first trial, X = 1. If it takes 5 trials before the first success shows up, X = 5. Because there's no upper limit on how long you might have to wait, X can in principle take any positive integer value: 1, 2, 3, 4, and onward forever. That's a sharp contrast with the binomial distribution, whose values were always capped between 0 and a fixed n.

The general formula for the geometric distribution is P(X = k) = (1 minus p)^(k minus 1) x p. The reasoning behind it is simpler than the binomial case in one respect: there is only one way for the first success to land exactly on trial k, namely (k minus 1) failures in a row followed immediately by a success. Order is not in question the way it was for the binomial distribution, because the success has to be last, so there's no combination or count of arrangements to multiply in, just the product of probabilities down that one specific sequence.

Flip a fair coin repeatedly until the first head appears, so p = 0.5. Then P(X=1) = 0.5, since the very first flip could be heads. P(X=2) = (0.5)^1 x 0.5 = 0.25, one tail followed by a head. P(X=3) = (0.5)^2 x 0.5 = 0.125, two tails then a head. P(X=4) = (0.5)^3 x 0.5 = 0.0625, three tails then a head.

Adding just these first four probabilities: 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.0625 = 0.9375. That leaves 0.0625, or 1/16, of the total probability spread across X = 5, 6, 7, and every larger value combined, an infinite tail that keeps shrinking but never quite reaches zero. Despite that infinite list of possible values, the geometric distribution is still a valid probability distribution in the sense required by any probability distribution: every probability is between 0 and 1, and the full infinite sum across all values of X adds up to exactly 1. The shape this produces is always the same basic pattern, tallest at X = 1 and steadily shrinking as X increases, sometimes called right skewed because of that long thinning tail toward larger values.
